**Emma Carol Hayes** [OBE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Officer of the Order of the British Empire") (born 18 October 1976) is an English professional [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") [manager](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manager_\(association_football\) "Manager \(association football\)") who is the head coach of the [United States women's national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team "United States women's national soccer team"). She was previously manager of [Chelsea Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_F.C._Women "Chelsea F.C. Women") from 2012 to 2024, winning seven [Women's Super League titles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Women's_Super_League "FA Women's Super League"), including five consecutively from [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%9320_FA_WSL "2019–20 FA WSL") to [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023%E2%80%9324_Women's_Super_League "2023–24 Women's Super League"). In 2024, she led the United States to a gold medal at the [Paris Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament"). She was awarded the inaugural [Women's Johan Cruyff Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johan_Cruyff_Trophy_\(France_Football\) "Johan Cruyff Trophy \(France Football\)") that year as the best coach in the women's game.
## Early life
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emma_Hayes&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]
Hayes was born in [Camden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Camden "London Borough of Camden"), London, and attended [Parliament Hill School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_Hill_School "Parliament Hill School").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-:2-3) She played for [Arsenal's academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_W.F.C._Academy "Arsenal W.F.C. Academy") as a [midfielder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midfielder "Midfielder") from 1988 to 1996,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-frontrowsoccer-4) but an ankle injury while on a ski trip when she was 17 ultimately ended her playing career. With football ruled out, Hayes studied European studies, Spanish, and sociology at [Liverpool Hope University College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Hope_University "Liverpool Hope University") and later read for a master's degree in intelligence and international affairs.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-wrack7-5)
## Career
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emma_Hayes&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]
While at Liverpool Hope, Hayes coached the women's football team from 1997 to 1999. In 1999, she moved back to London, helping develop youth players at [Croydon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlton_Athletic_W.F.C. "Charlton Athletic W.F.C.") and [Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_Palace_F.C._\(Women\) "Crystal Palace F.C. \(Women\)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-frontrowsoccer-4) In 2002, she became the manager of the [Long Island Lady Riders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_Rough_Riders_\(UWS\) "Long Island Rough Riders \(UWS\)") on [Long Island, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island,_New_York "Long Island, New York"), becoming the youngest coach in the league. In the [USL W-League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USL_W-League_\(1995%E2%80%932015\) "USL W-League \(1995–2015\)"), she led the team to finish first in the Northeast Division of the Eastern Conference,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-W-League-6) and was named as the league's coach of the season.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-USWNT_appointment-7) The team won their conference semi-final match 3–1 against the [New York Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Magic "New York Magic"), before losing 4–2 in the conference championship against the [Boston Renegades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Renegades "Boston Renegades").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-:3-8) She was appointed as the head coach for the [Iona Gaels women's team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iona_Gaels_women's_soccer "Iona Gaels women's soccer"), of [Iona College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iona_College_\(New_York\) "Iona College \(New York\)") in [New Rochelle, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Rochelle,_New_York "New Rochelle, New York"), on 22 January 2003,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-Iona-9) where she remained until the end of the 2005 season. 
She returned to England to become the assistant first team coach for [Arsenal Ladies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_W.F.C. "Arsenal W.F.C.") over 3 seasons between 2005 and 2008, during which time the team won 11 major trophies including three Women's Premier League titles, three FA Women's Cups and the [UEFA Women's Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006%E2%80%9307_UEFA_Women's_Cup "2006–07 UEFA Women's Cup"). At the same time, she was also the club's Academy director, overseeing the development of young players.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-Chelsea_profile-2)
Hayes joined the [Chicago Red Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Red_Stars "Chicago Red Stars") of [Women's Professional Soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Professional_Soccer "Women's Professional Soccer") as a manager on 15 May 2008.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-Hayes_relieved-10) After she was sacked in 2010,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-:4-11) she took up a technical director role at [Western New York Flash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_New_York_Flash "Western New York Flash") and advised them on transfers, helping to create a team that won the 2011 Women's Professional Soccer championship. After another stint as a consultant for [Washington Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Freedom_\(soccer\) "Washington Freedom \(soccer\)"), Hayes returned to London and worked for the family business, Covent Garden FX, a currency exchange.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-12)
### Chelsea
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emma_Hayes&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Chelsea")]
During the mid-season [2012 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics") break on 14 August 2012,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-Chelsea_appointment-13) [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_F.C._Women "Chelsea F.C. Women") hired Hayes as manager for the remainder of the [2012 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Chelsea_L.F.C._season "2012 Chelsea L.F.C. season")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-wrack7-5)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-2012-08-18-14) following the resignation of [Matt Beard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Beard "Matt Beard") to become manager at [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_F.C._Women "Liverpool F.C. Women").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-:5-15) Hayes managed her first match with Chelsea on 18 August 2012 in a 1–0 win at [Doncaster Rovers Belles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doncaster_Rovers_Belles_L.F.C. "Doncaster Rovers Belles L.F.C.").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-2012-08-18-14)
#### 2015 season
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emma_Hayes&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2015 season")]
After narrowly missing out on the 2014 FA WSL 1 title on the final day, Hayes oversaw a huge squad overhaul that bore witness to the addition of several arrivals. Swedish shot-stopper [Hedvig Lindahl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedvig_Lindahl "Hedvig Lindahl") and promising England centre-half [Millie Bright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millie_Bright "Millie Bright") were among the new recruits.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-:6-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-:7-17) [Marija Banusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marija_Banu%C5%A1i%C4%87 "Marija Banušić"), [Gemma Davison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemma_Davison "Gemma Davison") and [Niamh Fahey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niamh_Fahey "Niamh Fahey") also joined Chelsea, signing from [Kristianstads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristianstads_DFF "Kristianstads DFF"), [Liverpool Ladies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_L.F.C. "Liverpool L.F.C.") and [Arsenal Ladies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_W.F.C. "Arsenal W.F.C.") respectively.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-20) Later on in the season, Hayes won the race for Reading and England forward [Fran Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran_Kirby "Fran Kirby") for a British record fee.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-21) With the agonising memories of final-day defeat still fresh in memory, Hayes guided her side to a historic league and cup double, edging the FA Cup Final thanks to a lone strike from [Ji So-yun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ji_So-yun "Ji So-yun") late on in the first half.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-22) Later on in the season, they avenged themselves by winning the FA WSL 1 title, after hammering [Sunderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunderland_A.F.C._Ladies "Sunderland A.F.C. Ladies") at home 4–0 to secure the trophy.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-League_Tables-23)
In the [Women's Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Women's_Champions_League "UEFA Women's Champions League"), Hayes's side reached the last 16 after defeating [Glasgow City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow_City_F.C. "Glasgow City F.C."). After their 2–1 home defeat by [VfL Wolfsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VfL_Wolfsburg_\(women\) "VfL Wolfsburg \(women\)"), Hayes criticised [The Football Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Football_Association "The Football Association") for poor fixture scheduling, insisting that the competition is "geared to French, German and Swedish teams, and until we change that or listen to clubs like Chelsea we are always going to get knocked out in the early rounds."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-24)
#### 2016–17 season
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emma_Hayes&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2016–17 season")]
> "[Hayes] built everything at Chelsea – from having the kit washed to having food, to having our own building, to having our own training and pitches. Now, it’s an absolute professional setup but everything's been a fight over the years to do that."
— [Katie Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katie_Chapman "Katie Chapman"), who played under Hayes at three different clubs, credits her with building Chelsea from the ground-up.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-wrack7-5)
Hayes' side finished second in The FA WSL 1, five points adrift of Champions [Manchester City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_City_W.F.C. "Manchester City W.F.C.").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-League_Tables-23) The Blues also reached the FA Cup Final for the second consecutive year, losing 1–0 to a strong Arsenal side.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-25) Chelsea however won the [FA WSL Spring Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_WSL_Spring_Series "FA WSL Spring Series"), an interim edition of the FA WSL. Hayes led the side to first place, finishing on the same points as Manchester City but beating them on goal difference.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-26)
#### 2017–18 season
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emma_Hayes&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2017–18 season")]
Aided with the addition of new players including [Ramona Bachmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramona_Bachmann "Ramona Bachmann"), [Maren Mjelde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maren_Mjelde "Maren Mjelde"), [Erin Cuthbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erin_Cuthbert "Erin Cuthbert") and [Crystal Dunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_Dunn "Crystal Dunn"), Emma Hayes guided her side to finish top, in a reorganised FA WSL1, on goal difference.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
The team also played the FA Cup competitions and reached the semi-final but were knocked out by Birmingham City in a penalty shoot-out.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-27)
#### 2019–20 and 2020–21 seasons
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emma_Hayes&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2019–20 and 2020–21 seasons")]
> I enjoy representing a club I absolutely adore. To be in a position where we can continue to win on behalf of Chelsea is something I think I was born for.
— Hayes, reflecting on her success at Chelsea.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-28)
Hayes sought to rebuild the team at the conclusion of the 2017–18 season around new recruits [Sam Kerr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Kerr "Sam Kerr"), [Pernille Harder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pernille_Harder_\(footballer\) "Pernille Harder \(footballer\)"), [Melanie Leupolz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melanie_Leupolz "Melanie Leupolz"), [Magda Eriksson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magda_Eriksson "Magda Eriksson"), and [Ann Katrin Berger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Katrin_Berger "Ann Katrin Berger"), having moved on some key first-team players. The 2019–20 and 2020–21 season saw her team win back-to-back WSL titles[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-29) in what were record breaking years,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-chelsw2021-30) following a trophy-less 2018–19 campaign.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-wrack1-31) Given Chelsea's dominance in the 2020–21 season in both Europe and England,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-32) some observers hailed them as one of the best teams ever.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-wrack1-31)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-33) Hayes became the first woman manager to reach the Champions League final in 12 years.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-34) On 16 May, her Chelsea team, also playing their first-ever Champions League final, lost 4–0 to [Barcelona Femeni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona_Femeni "Barcelona Femeni").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-35)
Hayes won the 2020–21 FA WSL _Manager of the Season_ award.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-hayesobe-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-37) Two months later, she signed a new long-term contract with Chelsea.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-38) In the same year, Hayes was inducted into the FA WSL Hall of Fame.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-hayesobe-36) Based on the 2020–21 season, on 17 January 2022, she was adjudged [The Best FIFA Football Coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Best_FIFA_Football_Coach "The Best FIFA Football Coach"), beating off competition from [Lluís Cortés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llu%C3%ADs_Cort%C3%A9s "Lluís Cortés") and [Sarina Wiegman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarina_Wiegman "Sarina Wiegman").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-41)
#### 2023–24 season
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emma_Hayes&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2023–24 season")]
On 4 November 2023, Chelsea officially announced Hayes would depart after the ongoing season to “pursue a new opportunity outside of the WSL and club football.”[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-Emma_Hayes_to_depart_Chelsea-42) Reports in the United States indicated that Hayes was in advanced talks to become the new manager of the [United States women's national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team "United States women's national soccer team").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-44) On 14 November 2023, Hayes was named Head Coach of the United States women's national team starting at the conclusion of the [WSL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Super_League "Women's Super League") season.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-USWNT_appointment-7) On 21 January 2024, Hayes became the first woman to win the Football Writers Association Tribute Award in its 42 year history.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
Chelsea lost to Arsenal 1–0 after extra time at the [FA Women's League Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023%E2%80%9324_FA_Women's_League_Cup#Final "2023–24 FA Women's League Cup"). After the match, Hayes was seen to have shoved Arsenal head coach [Jonas Eidevall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonas_Eidevall "Jonas Eidevall") as they shook hands. Hayes claimed it was due to Eidevall's "unacceptable male aggression" on the touchline after an altercation with [Erin Cuthbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erin_Cuthbert "Erin Cuthbert") during the match.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-45) Chelsea went on to crash out of the [Women's FA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023%E2%80%9324_Women's_FA_Cup#Semi-finals "2023–24 Women's FA Cup") and [UEFA Women's Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023%E2%80%9324_UEFA_Women's_Champions_League_knockout_phase#SF_1.2 "2023–24 UEFA Women's Champions League knockout phase") in the semi-final stages but ultimately won a fifth WSL title in a row to send Hayes out on a high.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-47)
### United States
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emma_Hayes&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: United States")]
In November 2023, Hayes was named head coach of the [United States women's national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team "United States women's national soccer team") (USWNT) starting at the conclusion of the WSL season.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-USWNT_appointment-7) She began her tenure in May 2024 with only two months to prepare for [the Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-48) On 1 June, in the team's debut under Hayes and the first of four [friendlies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exhibition_game "Exhibition game") before the Olympics, the United States won 4–0 against [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team "South Korea women's national football team").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-49) Despite the short time she had with the team, she took them through an undefeated Olympics run, winning the gold medal game 1–0 against [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_women's_national_football_team "Brazil women's national football team") on 10 August. The team went 6–0 and scored its opponents 12–2 at the tournament.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-50) On 28 October, she was awarded the inaugural [Women's Johan Cruyff Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballon_d'Or "Ballon d'Or") as the best coach in the women's game.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-:8-51)
Before the next major tournament cycle, Hayes introduced the "WNT Way", a plan to develop the women's game in the United States through a unique "female lens".[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-52) Hayes saw her first loss with the USWNT on 26 February 2025, dropping 2–1 to [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_women's_national_football_team "Japan women's national football team") at the [2025 SheBelieves Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_SheBelieves_Cup "2025 SheBelieves Cup").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-53) She has broadened the USWNT player pool during her tenure, giving 17 players their USWNT debuts in her first 20 games, the most by a new manager since the early days of the program.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-54)
## Personal life
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emma_Hayes&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Personal life")]
In 2018, Hayes was pregnant with twins, but [lost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miscarriage "Miscarriage") one of them 28 weeks in.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-wrack7-5) She gave birth to the surviving twin on 17 May 2018.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-56)
Hayes credits [Vic Akers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_Akers "Vic Akers"), former [Arsenal W.F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_W.F.C. "Arsenal W.F.C.") manager under whom she was part of the backroom staff when they won an unprecedented [quadruple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_association_football_teams_to_have_won_four_or_more_trophies_in_one_season "List of association football teams to have won four or more trophies in one season") in the 2006–07 season, for being a "massive" influence on her career.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-57) Speaking of her experience coaching in the United States she said though she was born in England, she was "definitely made in America."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-58) In 2023, Hayes co-wrote a book, _Kill The Unicorn_ , which discusses high-performance management and argues that the perception of a single great leader is a myth.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-59)
Chelsea forward [Fran Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran_Kirby "Fran Kirby"), who suffered from severe depression after the loss of her mother early in her life and from a career-threatening illness in her late 20s, is particularly close to Hayes. Speaking of Hayes's positive influence in her life she said, "Emma's been incredible. She's been my rock; the person who made sure I was protected from everything."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-recov-60) Former Chelsea and England player, [Karen Carney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Carney "Karen Carney"), also praised Hayes for being there when she felt the most vulnerable and isolated.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-61)
Hayes was appointed [Member of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") (MBE) in the [2016 Birthday Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Birthday_Honours "2016 Birthday Honours"),[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-62) and was appointed Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the [2022 New Year Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_New_Year_Honours "2022 New Year Honours"), both for services to association football.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-63)
She is a [Tottenham Hotspur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tottenham_Hotspur_F.C. "Tottenham Hotspur F.C.") fan.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Hayes#cite_note-64)
